query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-treating Ti-6Al-4V alloy with laser shock peening (LSP) before subjecting it to low‐temperature vacuum ion–plasma nitriding will synergistically refine the near‐surface microstructure and generate elevated compressive residual stress that promotes more efficient nitrogen diffusion. This modification produces a more uniform, adherent, and less brittle nitride compound layer, ultimately increasing surface hardness and wear resistance without compromising fatigue life under cyclic and dynamic loading.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Ti-6Al-4V alloy with a Widmanstätten-type microstructure.
generation.intervention: A sequential two-step treatment: first apply laser shock peening (using moderate pulse energy to induce severe plastic deformation and grain refinement) and then perform low-temperature vacuum ion-plasma nitriding.
generation.conditions: Laboratory-scale tests conducted at room temperature under both dry sliding (e.g., pin-on-disk) and cyclic/fatigue loading conditions representative of structural service environments. Process parameters should be optimized within industrially relevant ranges (e.g., LSP energy adjusted to induce a surface layer of several hundred microns and nitriding at temperatures that avoid excessive brittleness).
generation.structural_mediator: A nitrogen-enriched sub-surface layer with a refined grain structure and enhanced compressive residual stresses that support the formation of a uniform Ti-N compound layer (comprising TiN and Ti2N) with improved adhesion.
generation.mechanism: Laser shock peening creates a highly deformed, fine-grained surface with elevated dislocation density and rich diffusion paths, as well as imposing deep compressive residual stresses. When subsequently nitrided at controlled low temperatures, these modified surface characteristics facilitate a more thorough and uniform diffusion of nitrogen into the substrate, ensuring that the resulting nitride layer not only achieves very high hardness but also remains well bonded with reduced brittleness and spalling tendencies.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid treatment is expected to yield a surface hardness increase that is an additional 20-30% higher than that achieved by conventional plasma nitriding alone and improve wear resistance by roughly 40-60% under cyclic and frictional loads. At the same time, the fatigue performance should be maintained or improved relative to plasma nitriding without LSP pre-treatment.
generation.baseline: Ti-6Al-4V alloy in the as-received state and a control group treated solely by low-temperature plasma nitriding.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected under moderate service conditions typical for structural applications; however, under extreme thermal or mechanical loads, or if the LSP parameters are not optimally tuned, the synergistic benefits may not manifest. Long-term stability and corrosion behavior need further evaluation.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds upon the established benefits of plasma nitriding for increasing hardness (PMC6384831::web::015::3_results_and_discussions) and the use of LSP to induce compressive stresses and grain refinement (PMC6073473::web::016::4_conclusions). The interaction between LSP-induced microstructural modifications and subsequent nitrogen diffusion is not well documented, so determining the optimal LSP and nitriding parameter window is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of Ti-6Al-4V samples: (1) untreated control, (2) samples receiving only low-temperature vacuum ion-plasma nitriding, and (3) samples that first undergo laser shock peening followed by the same nitriding treatment. All groups will be subjected to identical pin-on-disk wear testing and cyclic fatigue tests.
measurements: Wear rate and scar depth (via weight loss measurements and optical profilometry)
Microstructural evaluation (using SEM/EBSD to assess layer uniformity and grain refinement)
Fatigue life assessment under cyclic loading conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the LSP-nitrided samples do not exhibit at least a 20% further increase in surface hardness and a 40% reduction in wear rate compared to the nitriding-only group, or if there is any statistically significant degradation in fatigue life, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: LSP generated microdents on the surface of TC17 titanium alloy which induced plastic deformation and residual compressive stress on this material. The improvement in the impact-sliding wear resistance of TC17 titanium alloy after LSP was caused by the increased surface hardness and compressive residual stress. Under the same impact-sliding wear condition, the test sample treated by 7J pulse energy exhibited the best wear resistance, whereas the untreated sample showed the poorest results. As impact-sliding cycles increased, growth rates of wear area, wear depth, and wear volume of the three test samples varied. Therefore, lower growth rate was obtained when pulse energy was higher. The main wear mechanisms of the three test samples included delamination and abrasive wear.

By varying the microstructure and nitriding parameters, the fatigue strength of a material can be affected. Tokaji et al. [] reported that the fatigue strength of pure titanium was increased by nitriding, while it was decreased in the case of Ti-6Al-4V. Based on detailed observations of fatigue crack initiation, growth, and fracture surfaces, the improvement and the reduction in fatigue strength by nitriding of pure titanium and Ti-6Al-4V alloys were primarily attributed to enhanced crack initiation resistance and to premature crack initiation of the nitride layer, respectively. However, Farokhzadeh et al. [] achieved an improvement on the fatigue proprieties of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy plasma nitrided at a low temperature (600 °C). These results were different than those obtained by an elevated temperature treatment (900 °C) as well as conventional gas/plasma nitriding treatments reported in the literature [,,]. The thin morphology of the compound layer restricted the extent of premature crack initiation from the surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy.
